title: Putting the Tool in One Cell Type

scenes.visual: Deep navy canvas (#0B132B). Reusing the first film's colour map, the ice-blue neuron (#89CFF0, Neuron A) sits inside a tissue field beside soft violet neurons (#A78BFA, Neuron B) and muted slate neighbors. Title fades in crisp white (size 44): 'Putting the Tool in One Cell Type', then clears while the cells stay in place.

scenes.tts: In the first film, you met a glowing reporter and a light-gated actuator. In a brain with billions of cells, how do you put them into one chosen cell type? Almost every cell holds the same chromosomes, so control comes from where a gene is read.
scenes.caption: In the first film, you met a glowing reporter and a light-gated actuator. In a brain with billions of cells, how do you put them into one chosen cell type? Almost every cell holds the same chromosomes, so control comes from where a gene is read.
scenes.visual: Carry the tissue field (ice-blue Neuron A, violet Neuron B, slate neighbors) filling the upper 60% of the frame, with a small emerald reporter badge and coral actuator badge hovering above. Along the lower strip, a clean horizontal white chromosome track appears inside every cell, looking identical.
scenes.narration: In the first film, you met a glowing reporter and a light-gated actuator. In a brain with billions of cells, how do you put them into one chosen cell type? Almost every cell holds the same chromosomes, so control comes from where a gene is read.

scenes.tts: Start with a transgene, a piece of engineered D N A added to a fertilized egg. Every transgene pairs two parts. The promoter decides where and when a gene runs. The coding sequence decides which protein the cell builds.
scenes.caption: Start with a transgene, a piece of engineered DNA added to a fertilized egg. Every transgene pairs two parts. The promoter decides where and when a gene runs. The coding sequence decides which protein the cell builds.
scenes.visual: Enlarge the chromosome track at the bottom into a crisp two-block DNA bar: a light-gold bent arrow labeled 'Promoter: where & when' followed by an emerald block labeled 'Coding sequence: what is made'. A small glowing RNA wave smoothly glides off the coding block while labels stay size 30.
scenes.narration: Start with a transgene, a piece of engineered DNA added to a fertilized egg. Every transgene pairs two parts. The promoter decides where and when a gene runs. The coding sequence decides which protein the cell builds.

scenes.tts: Pair a promoter active in every cell with the green fluorescent protein gene. Every cell reads it, and you get a glowing green mouse. That proves a transgene works, yet every neuron lights up at once. You still cannot isolate one cell type.
scenes.caption: Pair a promoter active in every cell with the green fluorescent protein gene. Every cell reads it, and you get a glowing green mouse. That proves a transgene works, yet every neuron lights up at once. You still cannot isolate one cell type.
scenes.visual: Label the gold promoter arrow 'Active everywhere'. Light waves shoot from the DNA track up into the tissue field; Neuron A, Neuron B, and every slate neighbor all flood with emerald green (#2ECC71), and a schematic green mouse icon appears at top right. Then a soft amber ring highlights Neuron A alone, showing the mismatch.
scenes.narration: Pair a promoter active in every cell with the green fluorescent protein gene. Every cell reads it, and you get a glowing green mouse. That proves a transgene works, yet every neuron lights up at once. You still cannot isolate one cell type.

scenes.tts: To target one cell type cleanly, split the job across two genes. Put your reporter behind a strong promoter, then block it with a stop signal that halts reading. Flank that stop block with two short tags called lox P, pointing the same way. With the stop intact, every cell stays dark.
scenes.caption: To target one cell type cleanly, split the job across two genes. Put your reporter behind a strong promoter, then block it with a stop signal that halts reading. Flank that stop block with two short tags called loxP, pointing the same way. With the stop intact, every cell stays dark.
scenes.visual: All cells return to dark baseline colors (ice-blue, violet, slate). On the DNA track, insert a crimson 'STOP' block (#EF4444) between two gold rightward triangles ('loxP', 34 bp) right ahead of the emerald reporter block. A reading arrow starts at the promoter, bumps into the crimson STOP block, and bounces off.
scenes.narration: To target one cell type cleanly, split the job across two genes. Put your reporter behind a strong promoter, then block it with a stop signal that halts reading. Flank that stop block with two short tags called loxP, pointing the same way. With the stop intact, every cell stays dark.

scenes.tts: Now bring in a recombinase called Cre, an enzyme from a bacterial virus. A recombinase cuts and rejoins D N A, and Cre does it at lox P sites. Here is the twist. Cre turns a gene on by deleting D N A. It cuts out the stop block, clears the roadblock, and lets the cell build the tool.
scenes.caption: Now bring in a recombinase called Cre, an enzyme from a bacterial virus. A recombinase cuts and rejoins DNA, and Cre does it at loxP sites. Here is the twist. Cre turns a gene on by deleting DNA. It cuts out the stop block, clears the roadblock, and lets the cell build the tool.
scenes.visual: A teal ring-shaped enzyme cartoon ('Cre', #2DD4BF) glides onto both gold loxP triangles, loops the crimson STOP block upward, snips it away as a drifting circle, and rejoins the DNA leaving one loxP triangle. Now the reading arrow sails straight across into the emerald reporter block, which lights up.
scenes.narration: Now bring in a recombinase called Cre, an enzyme from a bacterial virus. A recombinase cuts and rejoins DNA, and Cre does it at loxP sites. Here is the twist. Cre turns a gene on by deleting DNA. It cuts out the stop block, clears the roadblock, and lets the cell build the tool.

scenes.tts: So which cells make Cre? Place the Cre gene behind a promoter active mainly in neuron type A. Type A makes Cre, snips out the stop, and lights up green. Neighboring cells never make Cre, keep their stop blocks, and stay dark.
scenes.caption: So which cells make Cre? Place the Cre gene behind a promoter active mainly in neuron type A. Type A makes Cre, snips out the stop, and lights up green. Neighboring cells never make Cre, keep their stop blocks, and stay dark.
scenes.visual: Show a second compact DNA track on the left labeled 'Type A promoter -> Cre'. Teal Cre icons appear inside the ice-blue Neuron A cells, excise their crimson STOP blocks, and fill Neuron A with bright emerald glow. Violet Neuron B and slate neighbors show intact STOP blocks and stay unlit.
scenes.narration: So which cells make Cre? Place the Cre gene behind a promoter active mainly in neuron type A. Type A makes Cre, snips out the stop, and lights up green. Neighboring cells never make Cre, keep their stop blocks, and stay dark.

scenes.tts: Pause here for a key consequence. Cre removed that stop block from neuron A's chromosome for good. Suppose that cell later divides, and its daughter cells stop making Cre. Do those daughter cells still make the glowing reporter?
scenes.caption: Pause here for a key consequence. Cre removed that stop block from neuron A's chromosome for good. Suppose that cell later divides, and its daughter cells stop making Cre. Do those daughter cells still make the glowing reporter?
scenes.visual: Focus on one ice-blue Neuron A cell splitting smoothly into two ice-blue daughter cells while the teal Cre icons fade out to zero. Inside both daughters, the tiny chromosome track clearly lacks the crimson STOP block. Question card slides in at top: 'Do daughter cells still make the reporter?'
scenes.narration: Pause here for a key consequence. Cre removed that stop block from neuron A's chromosome for good. Suppose that cell later divides, and its daughter cells stop making Cre. Do those daughter cells still make the glowing reporter?

scenes.visual: Hold the question card 'Do daughter cells still make the reporter?' above the two newly formed ice-blue daughter cells (no Cre present, stop-free chromosome tracks glowing faintly). Gentle ambient particle drift and a bottom progress bar mark the 4.5-second thinking pause.

scenes.tts: Yes, they do. Because the stop block is gone from the chromosome, every descendant inherits the unlocked gene. That permanent mark lets biologists trace cell lineages. Yet it carries a catch. Brief early Cre activity can unlock unintended cells too, so check every Cre line with a reporter.
scenes.caption: Yes, they do. Because the stop block is gone from the chromosome, every descendant inherits the unlocked gene. That permanent mark lets biologists trace cell lineages. Yet it carries a catch. Brief early Cre activity can unlock unintended cells too, so check every Cre line with a reporter.
scenes.visual: Both ice-blue daughter cells flare bright emerald green ('Lineage traced'). Then pan slightly right: one stray muted-slate neighbor also shows a faint emerald glow labeled 'Early leak? Check with reporter', keeping the visual as cautious as the narration.
scenes.narration: Yes, they do. Because the stop block is gone from the chromosome, every descendant inherits the unlocked gene. That permanent mark lets biologists trace cell lineages. Yet it carries a catch. Brief early Cre activity can unlock unintended cells too, so check every Cre line with a reporter.

scenes.tts: Need a second tool in neuron type B? Add flip, a yeast enzyme that cuts only its own sites. Drive Cre in type A and flip in type B, and each unlocks its own tool cleanly. Promoters and recombinases place each tool in chosen cells.
scenes.caption: Need a second tool in neuron type B? Add Flp, a yeast enzyme that cuts only its own sites. Drive Cre in type A and Flp in type B, and each unlocks its own tool cleanly. Promoters and recombinases place each tool in chosen cells.
scenes.visual: In the same tissue field, lavender enzyme icons ('Flp', #C084FC) appear in violet Neuron B and snip a STOP block between lavender diamond sites in front of the coral actuator (#FB7185). Now ice-blue Neuron A glows emerald (reporter) while violet Neuron B glows coral (actuator), with slate neighbors dark.
scenes.narration: Need a second tool in neuron type B? Add Flp, a yeast enzyme that cuts only its own sites. Drive Cre in type A and Flp in type B, and each unlocks its own tool cleanly. Promoters and recombinases place each tool in chosen cells.

scenes.visual: Deep navy canvas (#0B132B) with the faded two-color tissue field behind. Centered single white line (size 38, no subline beneath it): 'Promoters and recombinases place each tool in chosen cells.'
